common_name: Alister Stella Gray Rose (Yellow-to-Cream Climbing Noisette)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, with a trellis, fence, or arbor for the climbing canes; Alister Stella Gray, introduced in 1894, is a fragrant climbing Noisette well suited to Gulf Coast heat.

directions: Plant at the base of a trellis, fence, or arbor in well-drained soil in full sun, and tie in canes as they extend. Alister Stella Gray, introduced in 1894, bears small, high-centered, richly fragrant flowers that open golden-yellow and fade attractively to cream as they age, often showing several shades at once within a single cluster. It repeats reliably through the growing season on a moderately vigorous climber well suited to a large trellis, pillar, or fence, and like other Noisettes it tolerates Southern heat and humidity with good disease resistance. Train canes horizontally to encourage more flowering side shoots, and prune lightly after the main flush to maintain shape.

common_name: Louise Odier Rose (Fragrant Warm-Pink Bourbon Rose)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Louise Odier, a Bourbon rose from 1851, performs well in the heat and humidity of Southern gardens with good repeat bloom.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Louise Odier, introduced in 1851, is a classic Bourbon rose bearing warm rose-pink, cupped, densely petaled flowers with an exceptionally strong, rich fragrance, produced in generous flushes through the growing season on an upright, well-branched shrub. Bourbon roses like this one bridge the gap between antique once-blooming roses and modern repeat-flowering hybrids, and Louise Odier remains one of the most fragrant and reliable of the class for warm-climate gardens. Feed and water a bit more generously than tougher China or Tea roses, since Bourbons appreciate slightly richer soil, and prune lightly after each bloom flush to encourage continued rebloom.

common_name: Baronne Prevost Rose (Extremely Hardy Antique Hybrid Perpetual)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Baronne Prevost, introduced in 1842, is an extremely cold-hardy Hybrid Perpetual rose that also performs well in warm Southern gardens.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Baronne Prevost, introduced in 1842, is one of the earliest Hybrid Perpetual roses and remains prized for its extreme hardiness and large, deep rose-pink, flat, quartered blooms densely packed with petals in the old-fashioned style, carrying a strong classic rose fragrance. Its wide climate tolerance, from cold northern winters to hot Southern summers, has kept it a mainstay of heirloom rose collections for over 180 years. It blooms in a strong spring flush with some repeat through summer and fall, and benefits from richer soil and more regular feeding than tougher China or Tea roses. Prune moderately in late winter to shape and remove old wood, and deadhead spent blooms to encourage additional flowering.

common_name: Katharina Zeimet Rose (White Baby Rambler Polyantha)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Katharina Zeimet, a 1901 polyantha nicknamed the White Baby Rambler, blooms nearly continuously on a compact, low-maintenance plant.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light afternoon shade. Katharina Zeimet, introduced in 1901 and nicknamed the White Baby Rambler, is a compact polyantha rose bearing large clusters of small, pure white, lightly fragrant flowers almost continuously from spring through frost. Its low, dense, well-behaved habit makes it a reliable choice for borders, edging, and mass plantings, needing far less spraying and maintenance than many modern roses to look good all season. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and remove dead wood, and expect vigorous rebloom within a few weeks after each flush is spent.

common_name: Fortune's Double Yellow Rose (Antique Coppery-Orange Climber)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, with a warm, sheltered site and a fence or wall to climb; Fortune's Double Yellow, brought from China in 1845, blooms once heavily in spring and needs a mild winter climate to perform its best.

directions: Plant against a warm, sheltered wall, fence, or trellis in well-drained soil in full sun. Fortune's Double Yellow, also called Beauty of Glazenwood, was introduced from a Chinese garden in 1845 and remains treasured for its unusual coppery orange-and-yellow semi-double blooms, a color combination unlike almost any other antique rose, opening from buds flushed crimson. It flowers in a single spectacular spring flush on a vigorous climbing plant, performing best in the mild winters of zone 7 and warmer where its tender growth is not cut back by hard freezes. Give it a warm, protected site such as a south-facing wall, and prune only lightly right after the spring bloom to preserve as much of the flowering wood as possible for next year.

common_name: Mermaid Rose (Vigorous Single Pale-Yellow Evergreen Climber)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root roses in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, with a very sturdy structure to climb; Mermaid, introduced in 1918, is an extremely vigorous, nearly evergreen climbing rose that can eventually cover a large wall, fence, or outbuilding.

directions: Plant at the base of a very sturdy fence, wall, or arbor in well-drained soil in full sun, since Mermaid grows into an exceptionally large, heavy climber that needs substantial support. Introduced in 1918 as a hybrid of Rosa bracteata, Mermaid bears large, single, pale primrose-yellow flowers with prominent amber stamens over a long bloom season from late spring well into fall, on a vigorous, nearly evergreen, thorny plant that can climb 20 feet or more given time and the right support. It tolerates heat, humidity, and poor soil better than most climbing roses and shows excellent disease resistance, but its size and vicious thorns mean it is best sited where it has plenty of room to grow and is not near a walkway. Once established it needs little pruning beyond removing dead wood and controlling its spread.
